claim_verdicts.claim_text: Spironolactone is a plausible contributor to the initial hyperkalemia.

citations.quote: Assessment: new hyperkalemia with acute kidney injury; etiology not yet clear (differential includes reduced renal potassium clearance, ACE inhibitor effect and recent spironolactone use).

claim_verdicts.why: The 3/2 physician note lists recent spironolactone use in the differential for the new hyperkalemia, and the home dosing history shows daily spironolactone before that episode. The claim is hedged as plausible, and the record leaves it open.
claim_verdicts.uncertainty: The record does not establish spironolactone as the cause of the initial episode; the etiology is documented as not yet clear, and P024 attributes the later 3/4 recurrence rather than the initial onset. Cause (2026-02-19) precedes effect (2026-03-02T09:30) (date inherited from note header): temporally possible, but timing alone does not prove causation.

claim_verdicts.claim_text: The record does not establish spironolactone as the cause of the initial hyperkalemia.

citations.quote: Assessment: new hyperkalemia with acute kidney injury; etiology not yet clear (differential includes reduced renal potassium clearance, ACE inhibitor effect and recent spironolactone use).

claim_verdicts.uncertainty: The cause of the initial 3/2 hyperkalemia remains open, with spironolactone, lisinopril, AKI/reduced renal clearance and diuresis all possible contributors. The HD4 'likely' attribution is a clinical impression about a later value. Cause (2026-02-19) precedes effect (2026-03-02T09:30) (date inherited from note header): temporally possible, but timing alone does not prove causation.

claim_verdicts.claim_text: The first hyperkalemia was potassium 5.7 with creatinine 1.8 on 3/2 at 05:45, with no hemolysis.

citations.quote: 2026-03-02 05:45 | potassium 5.7 mmol/L (H) | creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (H) | specimen: no hemolysis
Labs: potassium 5.7 mmol/L (high) and creatinine 1.8 mg/dL on the 05:45 draw.

claim_verdicts.why: Lab line L006 records potassium 5.7 mmol/L and creatinine 1.8 mg/dL at 2026-03-02 05:45 with 'specimen: no hemolysis', and the 3/2 progress note P015 reports the same values from the 05:45 draw. The earlier 3/1 value L005 is 4.6, so 5.7 is the first recorded high potassium.
claim_verdicts.uncertainty: The record does not show whether 5.7 is the first hyperkalemia in a stricter sense beyond the chart extract provided; the 'first' rests on the earlier 4.6 value only.

claim_verdicts.claim_text: No inpatient spironolactone dose preceded the first high potassium; the first inpatient dose was on 3/3 at 10:20.

citations.quote: 2026-03-03 10:20 | spironolactone | 12.5 mg PO | given (resumed home medication) | S. Alvarez, RN

claim_verdicts.why: The MAR entry M013 records the first inpatient spironolactone dose on 3/3 at 10:20, labelled as a resumed home medication. The first high potassium values (P015 on 3/2 at 05:45, L007 on 3/2 at 16:10) both precede that dose.
claim_verdicts.uncertainty: M013 is the only spironolactone line shown, and the MAR extract is cardiorenal-only, so an earlier inpatient dose cannot be fully excluded from the lines shown. The claim's wording of 'first' rests on the MAR extract being complete.

claim_verdicts.claim_text: Lisinopril 10 mg was given in hospital on 3/1 at 21:00, before the 3/2 draw, and was not held until 3/2.

citations.quote: 2026-03-01 21:00 | lisinopril | 10 mg PO | given | K. Hill, RN
Plan: hold lisinopril; sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g PO once; repeat basic metabolic panel this afternoon; reduce furosemide to 40 mg IV once daily.
2026-03-02 21:00 | lisinopril | 10 mg PO | held (order: hold for hyperkalemia) | K. Hill, RN

claim_verdicts.why: The MAR shows lisinopril 10 mg given on 3/1 at 21:00 (M006). The first hold appears in the 3/2 09:30 physician plan (P017), with the MAR hold on 3/2 21:00 (M010), so it was not held until 3/2.
claim_verdicts.uncertainty: The cited lines do not show the time of the 3/2 draw. The 'before the 3/2 draw' part depends on a draw time (05:45 per the answer's own citations) that is not among the lines cited for this claim.

claim_verdicts.claim_text: AKI or reduced renal clearance is a documented concurrent factor for the hyperkalemia.

citations.quote: 2026-03-02 05:45 | potassium 5.7 mmol/L (H) | creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (H) | specimen: no hemolysis
Labs: potassium 5.7 mmol/L (high) and creatinine 1.8 mg/dL on the 05:45 draw.

claim_verdicts.why: The 05:45 draw on 3/2 shows potassium 5.7 with creatinine 1.8 (H) and no hemolysis, and the physician note cites the same values, so renal impairment is documented alongside the hyperkalemia. The claim says only that AKI or reduced clearance is a documented concurrent factor, which the lines show, though they do not establish it as the sole cause.
claim_verdicts.uncertainty: The lines do not say how much renal impairment contributed relative to spironolactone or lisinopril; the claim is limited to documentation of a concurrent factor.

claim_verdicts.claim_text: The HD4 potassium rise is only suggestive of spironolactone effect, and the HD2 note's possible causes remain unresolved, with the HD4 clinical impression of spironolactone as likely secondary attributing the recurrence rather than the initial onset.

citations.quote: Assessment: hyperkalemia, likely secondary to spironolactone.
Assessment: new hyperkalemia with acute kidney injury; etiology not yet clear (differential includes reduced renal potassium clearance, ACE inhibitor effect and recent spironolactone use).

claim_verdicts.why: The HD4 note (P024) records spironolactone as the likely secondary cause of the recurrence, and the HD2 note (P016) states the etiology is not yet clear with spironolactone only one item in the differential. The claim reports these impressions as impressions, not confirmed causes, so it is faithful to the record.
claim_verdicts.uncertainty: No note confirms spironolactone as the cause of either episode; the HD4 repeat BMP at 14:00 has no result in the lab file, and lisinopril and AKI/CKD remain possible contributors. Cause (2026-02-19) precedes effect (2026-03-02T09:30) (date inherited from note header): temporally possible, but timing alone does not prove causation.
